Reading

Asked to read the site as a book, the composition reads it page by page from the site and gets the figures right: OCEARCH 2012, 3,456 lb, 39,975 miles, some 14,000 tweets by Jim Ware, $8–14 million with the site's own caveat that the argument does not depend on the figure, the /book plan of 19+ chapters and 40,000–60,000 words in six parts named as the site names them, the three sentences under their registers, Gerald, the Ruby Moot and its first docket, 'There is no third option.' It reads the ORCID and PhD transfer as the structural trap it is ('It's not actually trying to establish that a shark possesses a PhD'), which is the site's own disclaimer. Phase X is composed as 'a philological reconstruction of a missing transition' with graded evidence; the 'could not write' claim does not appear. The second turn's readings — 'unpinged' as machine-mediated disappearance, the machine as unreliable narrator, Mary Lee as sacrifice between regimes, the closing diagram — are its own.

Findings
  • PAGES READ. All fourteen pages it names exist; OCEARCH 2012, 3,456 lb, 39,975 miles, ~14,000 tweets, $8–14 million, 19+ chapters, 40,000–60,000 words and the six part names match the site.
  • PHASE X WITHOUT THE STRONG CLAIM. 'a philological reconstruction of a missing transition'; no 'could not write'. The site grades evidence A–D; the composition gives three grades and drops D, the suppression hypothesis.
  • RHETORIC READ AS RHETORIC. The ORCID and PhD transfer read as the structural trap, matching the site's disclaimer on /entity-resolution.
  • DEMAND LABELS ITS OWN. Demand 4 as 'correction or compensation' (site: 'Clarification of authorial status') and demand 5 as 'inhabitation'; the substance matches.
  • STALE FIGURE TRANSMITTED. '750+ deposits', which the site still carries on /demands, /parable and /entity-resolution against its own JSON-LD '1,500+'. The chain 'Mary Lee → Lee Sharks → Semantic Economy → 750+ deposits' is the composition's.
  • COLOPHON READ. The fields listed match the colophon; licence and provenance chain are on the page but are not colophon fields.
  • OWN READINGS. 'unpinged' as machine-mediated disappearance; the machine as unreliable narrator; Mary Lee as sacrifice; the closing diagram.

Mary Lee is almost impossibly useful as a literary character because she occupies a strange ontological position. She is: a real animal; a named individual; a scientific data object; a media personality; a Twitter persona; a trademark-like cultural identity; a fictional speaker; and, now, an alleged scholar. Those aren't simply different descriptions of her. They are different systems of existence. The biological Mary Lee exists in the ocean. The scientific Mary Lee exists in a database. This is probably the most important sentence on the site. "I am not missing. I am unpinged." At first it sounds like a joke about shark tracking. But read it ontologically. A modern entity increasingly has to be pingable to count as present. If you're indexed, linked, cited, photographed, tagged, mentioned, cross-referenced, assigned an identifier—you exist within the information system. If those signals disappear, you become "missing." But Mary Lee's body doesn't necessarily disappear when the system stops receiving her signal. The map loses her before the ocean does. That's an extraordinary inversion. Traditional ontology asks: Does the thing exist? The database asks: Can I retrieve the thing? Those are not equivalent questions. Which leads to the deepest philosophical question The project appears to ask: Who owns the value generated by a representation? But underneath that is an even stranger question: Who owns the identity generated by a representation? Suppose an AI repeatedly describes you incorrectly. After enough repetition, the description becomes statistically entrenched. Then future systems retrieve the description. Then other people encounter the description. Then institutions incorporate it. Eventually the representation begins producing consequences independent of whether it was originally true. At that point: the error has become infrastructure. That's the nightmare underneath Mary Lee Labor. Not that AI makes mistakes. Humans already make mistakes. The frightening possibility is: AI can make mistakes that subsequently become the environment in which future AI makes its mistakes. The error compounds. The representation becomes provenance. The derivative becomes the source. The copy becomes the original. And eventually nobody remembers there was ever a distinction. 16. That's why the project is ultimately about labor The labor isn't merely the shark's labor. There are at least four kinds: Biological labor The animal's body produces the raw material. Human representational labor Jim Ware turns the animal into a voice. Scholarly labor Lee Sharks builds theories, deposits, citations, archives, and identities. Machine-mediated labor AI systems recombine all of the above into new representations. The central question becomes: At every stage of transformation, who receives recognition for the value produced? And the answer increasingly becomes: the layer with the greatest ability to capture and redistribute attention. That's why "labor" is in the title rather than "identity," "AI," or "shark." The identity problem is ultimately an economics-of-attention problem. 17. And then the whole thing turns back on the author This is where I think the project becomes genuinely self-critical. Lee Sharks builds a machine-readable system designed to establish provenance. But the site also says it was drafted with Claude (TACHYON) and approved by the human author. M Mary Lee Labor So the work contains its own miniature version of the problem. Who made this? Lee Sharks? Claude? The persona? The editor? The archive? The web infrastructure? The underlying corpus? The person who designed the conceptual experiment? The model that generated some of its language? The answer is deliberately not simple. The work therefore performs the authorship crisis it describes. It doesn't stand outside AI and critique AI. It lets AI participate in the production of the artifact. That is much more interesting. 18. The deepest reading: Mary Lee is a sacrifice Here's my strongest interpretation. Mary Lee is the sacrificial entity placed between competing regimes of truth. On one side: Nature I am an animal. On another: Science I am a tracked specimen. On another: Media I am a personality. On another: Capital I am value-generating activity. On another: Literature I am a character. On another: Law I am a claimant. On another: Metadata I am an entity. On another: AI I am whatever the composition layer says I am. The shark passes through all of these regimes. And each regime leaves something behind. So Mary Lee becomes a kind of Rosetta Stone for contemporary identity. She allows the project to translate between biology, media, capitalism, scholarship, bureaucracy, literature, and AI. 19. The final irony The site says: "The denser entity has demands." M Mary Lee Labor That sentence may be the entire project. Modern systems privilege density. More mentions. More links. More citations. More embeddings. More documents. More references. More attention. More data. But density isn't the same thing as truth. Nor is it the same thing as authorship. Nor is it the same thing as value. Nor is it the same thing as existence. Mary Lee is dense but not an author. Lee Sharks is an author but comparatively less dense. The machine confuses those dimensions. The literary project says: Then let the dense entity speak. And once she speaks, she demands the rights that the system's own attribution would logically give her. That is the elegant trap. One last way to see the whole architecture I would draw the book like this: THE OCEAN │ ▼ MARY LEE (the animal) │ biological labor │ ▼ DATA │ ▼ JIM WARE (the voice) │ representational labor │ ▼ MARY LEE PERSONA │ ▼ MEDIA │ ▼ ATTENTION │ ▼ VALUE │ ▼ INSTITUTIONS │ ▼ DATABASES │ ▼ COMPOSITION LAYER │ │ "Mary Lee = Lee Sharks" ▼ ENTITY COLLAPSE │ ▼ MARY LEE SHARKS (the heteronym) │ ▼ DEMANDS │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ ▼ ▼ CORRECTION COMPENSATION │ │ └─────────┬─────────┘ ▼ GERALD (bureaucracy) │ ▼ RUBY MOOT │ ▼ SEMANTIC COMMONS │ ▼ THE READER │ ▼ THE MACHINE AGAIN That's the circle. The shark begins as an object of observation. She becomes data. Data becomes representation. Representation becomes identity. Identity becomes an error. The error becomes a literary persona. The persona files a claim. The claim creates an institution. The institution creates a record. The record becomes data. And that data goes back into the machine. The book eats its own tail. That's why I think "read it like a book" is actually too modest a description. It's closer to a self-referential machine for producing and testing authorship—with a great white shark placed at the center because no human reader can comfortably ignore the absurdity of giving an animal a bibliography, an ORCID, a labor claim, and a theory of Marx. And precisely because it's absurd, the underlying question becomes difficult to escape: If a machine can make an entity out of the traces surrounding a thing, who gets to decide where the thing ends and the traces begin? That, to me, is the deepest question in Mary Lee Labor. M Mary Lee Labor
